newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Africa gets two cheers for economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: Africa gets two cheers for economic reforms.

text.p: Sub-Saharan Africa, currently enjoying the best growth rates in two decades, received two cheers from economists and investors for recent reforms at a World Economic Forum (WEF) conference this week.
But the heads of state and finance ministers were told they had to accelerate the pace of free-market reform to compete effectively in an increasingly tough global market.

"This region has to become more competitive in manufactures -- that means lowering tariffs and opening borders," Jeffry Sachs, director of the Harvard Institute for International Development, said on Wednesday.

The continent's average real growth rate has increased from less than one percent in 1992 to over 5.5 percent in 1996. But the rise has largely been in the primary products sector, particularly agriculture, reflecting good rains in several countries and an upswing in commodity prices.
Manufacturing remains a disappointment with foreign investment into the region only a trickle compared to the flood of dollars which have flowed into other emerging markets.

David Robins, regional chief executive at Union Bank of Switzerland, said foreign direct investment into Southern Africa averaged just $90 million per country in 1995 compared to nearly $4.5 billion for Hungary.

"These figures imply that there is a serious investment barrier in this region...circumstantial evidence suggests that regulation and a lack of competition are helping to keep Southern Africa an expensive region to do business," he said.
Robins said African states needed to deregulate their telecommunications and transport sectors as a matter of urgency and accelerate plans to develop regional free trade zones.
Martin Shaw, chief executive of Deloitte and Touche, South Africa, also urged them to adopt a more flexible approach to labour policies.
African states -- with varying degrees of enthusiasm -- have in the 1990s by and large adopted the policies demanded by international investors and Bretton Woods institutions.
But the pace of reform in areas ranging from privatisation to exchange control liberalisation to curbing government spending has been patchy.
Alassane Ouattara, deputy ,managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), said there was a danger that regions within Africa would be held back by foot-dragging by some countries.
"The pace of progress should be what is feasible, not what is comfortable for the slowest member," he said.

Privatisation is a case in point with Zambia having already sold 200 state concerns and pushing ahead now with the sale of the pivotal copper industry while many of its neighbours are still only discussing the idea.
"We don't care who buys the mines in Zambia as long as the mines make a profit and contribute to the coffers of the state," said Zambian President Frederick Chiluba.

Callisto Madavo, World Bank vice-president responsible for Africa, said that Africa should now embrace privatisation having come late to a concept already well established in Latin America and Eastern Europe.

South Africa's peaceful post-apartheid transition has underpinned stability in the southern cone and political leaders hope the new government of Laurent Kabila in former Zaire will promote investor-friendly policies in Africa's third largest country.

But Africa still faces an uphill struggle, evidenced by the WEF's latest World Competitiveness report showing only two African countries among the world's top 53 competitive nations, with South Africa ranking 44th and Zimbabwe 51st.
The rankings leave Africa lagging far behind the Tiger economies of East Asia. But it does represent some progress.
"Zimbabwe would not have been in the top 53 countries in the world a few years ago," said Sachs.
